notes: Universal, neutral, works any time of day with anyone. In texts people stretch it ('holaaa') or pair it with an emoji.

examples.tl: Hola, ¿cómo estás?
examples.en: Hi, how are you?

notes: Neutral-casual greeting used everywhere. Also '¿Qué tal + noun?' = how was/is X ('¿Qué tal el viaje?').

examples.tl: ¿Qué tal tu día?
examples.en: How was your day?

notes: The standard. Use '¿Cómo está?' with older people, officials, your landlord. Reply 'Bien, ¿y tú?'.

examples.tl: Hola, señora, ¿cómo está?
examples.en: Hello ma'am, how are you?
examples.casual: Hola, ¿cómo estás? Hace rato que no te veo.

notes: Mexican slang, very common among friends (also '¿Qué ondas?'). Casual only; not for your boss or an official. Understood but less used elsewhere.

examples.tl: ¿Qué onda, güey? ¿Vas a ir hoy?
examples.en: What's up, dude? Are you going today?

notes: Casual, neutral across countries, a bit less common than '¿Qué tal?'. Longer form '¿Qué hay de nuevo?' = what's new.

examples.tl: ¿Qué hay? ¿Cómo va todo?
examples.en: What's up? How's everything going?

notes: Literally 'what happened', but in Mexico it is also a plain casual greeting. Context and tone tell you which one.

examples.tl: ¿Qué pasó? ¿Por qué no llegaste?
examples.en: What happened? Why didn't you show up?

notes: Neutral and warm, fine with friends or acquaintances. '¿Cómo le va?' for usted. Often asks about a specific thing: '¿Cómo te va en la chamba?'.

examples.tl: ¿Cómo te va en el nuevo departamento?
examples.en: How's it going in the new apartment?
examples.casual: ¿Cómo te va en el depa nuevo?

notes: The classic WhatsApp opener to start a chat. Reply 'Nada, aquí nomás' or 'Trabajando'.

examples.tl: ¿Qué haces? ¿Quieres ir por un café?
examples.en: What are you doing? Want to get a coffee?

notes: Until about noon or lunch. 'Buen día' (singular) is very common in Mexico and Argentina. Say it to strangers when entering a shop or elevator.

examples.tl: Buenos días, ¿me da dos tamales, por favor?
examples.en: Good morning, can I get two tamales, please?

notes: From lunchtime until dark (roughly 1–7 pm). Mexicans often switch to 'tardes' after comida, around 2 pm.

examples.tl: Buenas tardes, vengo a recoger un paquete.
examples.en: Good afternoon, I'm here to pick up a package.

notes: Both a greeting after dark and a farewell at bedtime. Pair with 'descansa' (rest well) when it is goodbye.

examples.tl: Buenas noches, ya me voy a dormir. Mañana hablamos.
examples.en: Good night, I'm going to bed. We'll talk tomorrow.
examples.casual: Buenas noches, ya me duermo. Mñn hablamos.

notes: Short for buenos días/tardes/noches. Neutral and extremely common when you walk into a store, a taxi or a WhatsApp group.

examples.tl: Buenas, ¿tiene cambio de quinientos?
examples.en: Hi, do you have change for five hundred?

notes: Default answer to any greeting, and as a question '¿Todo bien?' = you ok? Neutral everywhere.

examples.tl: ¿Todo bien? Te vi medio serio.
examples.en: Everything ok? You looked kind of serious.

notes: Mexican colloquial answer to '¿cómo estás?' meaning 'I'm managing'. Modest, slightly tired tone. Also 'ahí vamos' (same idea, more general).

examples.tl: —¿Cómo vas con la mudanza? —Ahí la llevo.
examples.en: —How's the move going? —Getting there.
examples.casual: Ahí la llevo, ya casi acabo.

notes: Mexican/Central American reply to '¿qué haces?'. 'Nomás' = nada más (just). Relaxed, friendly.

examples.tl: —¿Qué haces? —Aquí nomás, descansando.
examples.en: —What are you doing? —Just here, resting.

notes: The most common casual goodbye everywhere. Add a time: 'nos vemos mañana', 'nos vemos a las 8'.

examples.tl: Bueno, nos vemos el sábado entonces.
examples.en: Ok, see you Saturday then.

en: see you there / catch you later
notes: Mexican. Literally 'we'll see each other there', used both for a real meetup and as a vague 'later'. Also used to end a call.

examples.tl: Sale, ahí nos vemos en el metro Insurgentes.
examples.en: Ok, see you there at Insurgentes metro.
examples.casual: Sale, ahí nos vemos en el metro.

notes: Warm goodbye, used with friends and family. 'Cuídese' for usted. Very common at the end of calls and chats.

examples.tl: Ya me voy, cuídate mucho y avísame cuando llegues.
examples.en: I'm leaving, take care and let me know when you arrive.
examples.casual: Ya me voy, cuídate y avísame cuando llegues.

notes: Said to the person who is leaving. Neutral; 'que le vaya bien' for usted (shopkeepers say it to you). Reply 'Igualmente' or 'Gracias'.

examples.tl: Gracias por venir, que te vaya bien.
examples.en: Thanks for coming, take care.
examples.casual: Gracias x venir, q te vaya bien.

notes: Neutral-polite goodbye, the safe choice with strangers, clerks, officials. Friends more often say 'nos vemos' or 'bye'.

examples.tl: Gracias, hasta luego.
examples.en: Thanks, see you later.

notes: Borrowed English 'bye' is normal in Mexico and much of Latin America, especially among young people and in texts. Often 'bye bye' or 'byeee'.

examples.tl: Bueno, bye, nos vemos mañana.
examples.en: Ok, bye, see you tomorrow.

notes: How you announce you are leaving a place or a chat. 'Ya' here means 'now / finally'. Also 'me voy' or 'me retiro' (more formal).

examples.tl: Ya me voy, se me hace tarde para el trabajo.
examples.en: I'm leaving, I'm running late for work.
examples.casual: Ya me voy, se me hace tarde.

notes: From Italian 'ciao'. The default casual goodbye in Colombia, Chile, Peru, Venezuela. Understood in Mexico but Mexicans say 'bye' or 'adiós' more.

examples.tl: Listo, chao, hablamos luego.
examples.en: Alright, bye, talk later.

notes: Colombia's everyday greeting (literally 'what else?'). Also '¿Quiubo?' / '¿Qué hubo?'. In Mexico '¿qué más?' just means 'what else?'.

examples.tl: ¿Qué más, parce? ¿Bien o no?
examples.en: What's up, man? Doing good?

en: how did you sleep? / morning greeting
notes: Literally 'how did you dawn?'. Common morning greeting in Mexico and Central America, especially to someone you live with or text daily.

examples.tl: Buenos días, mi amor, ¿cómo amaneciste?
examples.en: Good morning love, how did you sleep?

notes: Bounce the question back. '¿Y usted?' when being polite. Skipping it can sound curt.

examples.tl: —¿Cómo estás? —Bien, gracias, ¿y tú?
examples.en: —How are you? —Good, thanks, and you?

notes: The number-one filler. Starts answers ('Pues no sé'), softens, or just buys time. In Mexican speech often shortened to 'pus'/'pos'; in texts 'ps'.

examples.tl: Pues yo creo que mejor vamos mañana.
examples.en: Well, I think we'd better go tomorrow.
examples.casual: Ps yo creo q mejor mñn.

notes: As a filler it opens or closes a topic ('Bueno, me voy'). Mexicans also answer the phone with '¿Bueno?'. Neutral everywhere.

examples.tl: Bueno, entonces nos vemos a las siete.
examples.en: Ok, so we'll see each other at seven.

notes: Used to rephrase or clarify; overused as 'like' by young people (stereotypically 'fresas'). Neutral across countries.

examples.tl: Llego tarde, o sea, como a las nueve.
examples.en: I'll be late, I mean, around nine.
examples.casual: Llego tarde, o sea como a las 9.

notes: The Spanish 'um'. Spoken only, not in texts. Stretch it ('esteee') while you think of the word. Using it makes you sound more natural than silence.

examples.tl: Quiero… este… la cosa para abrir latas.
examples.en: I want… um… the thing for opening cans.

notes: Gets attention before you explain something. 'Mire' for usted. Not rude, but in an argument tone it can sound confrontational.

examples.tl: Mira, si no te gusta el depa, buscamos otro.
examples.en: Look, if you don't like the apartment, we'll find another.
examples.casual: Mira, si no te late el depa, buscamos otro.

notes: Starts a request or question to someone you address as tú. 'Oiga' for usted (also how you call a waiter or get a stranger's attention).

examples.tl: Oye, ¿me pasas el número del plomero?
examples.en: Hey, can you send me the plumber's number?
examples.casual: Oye, ¿me pasas el num del plomero?

notes: Very Mexican way to introduce news or an excuse. 'Fíjese que' for usted. Also 'fíjate' alone = pay attention / look.

examples.tl: Fíjate que el casero ya no quiere renovar el contrato.
examples.en: Turns out the landlord doesn't want to renew the lease.
examples.casual: Fíjate q el casero ya no quiere renovar.

notes: Tag question at the end of a statement, the equivalent of 'right?'. Universal and very frequent in speech and texts.

examples.tl: Tú ya pagaste la luz, ¿no?
examples.en: You already paid the electric bill, right?

notes: Slightly softer than '¿no?' and a bit more polite. Also '¿Verdad?' alone = 'Right?' / 'I know, right?'. Mexicans sometimes say '¿verdá?'.

examples.tl: Hoy no hay clases, ¿verdad?
examples.en: There's no class today, right?

notes: As a tag it seeks agreement ('¿sí?' = ok?). Rising '¿Sí?' alone = 'oh really?'. Also how many answer the phone in Colombia/Argentina ('¿Aló?/¿Sí?').

examples.tl: Me avisas cuando llegues, ¿sí?
examples.en: Let me know when you get there, ok?

notes: Neutral everywhere. As a statement 'en serio' = seriously / for real ('Te lo digo en serio').

examples.tl: ¿En serio te cobraron mil pesos por el taxi?
examples.en: They seriously charged you a thousand pesos for the taxi?
examples.casual: ¿En serio te cobraron 1000 x el taxi?

notes: Mexican slang, casual only. 'La neta' = the truth; '¿Neta?' = for real?; 'neta que sí' = for real yes. Not used much outside Mexico.

examples.tl: ¿Neta ya te vas a Colombia? ¿Cuándo?
examples.en: For real you're moving to Colombia? When?

notes: Mexican slang: 'La neta, no me gustó' = honestly, I didn't like it. Also a compliment: 'eres la neta' = you're the best. Casual register.

examples.tl: La neta, el servicio del banco está pésimo.
examples.en: Honestly, the bank's service is terrible.
examples.casual: La neta el banco está pésimo.

notes: Mexican. The polite version of 'no mames'; fine with friends, coworkers, even some family. Expresses surprise, disbelief or 'stop messing around'.

examples.tl: ¡No manches! ¿Te subieron la renta otra vez?
examples.en: No way! They raised your rent again?
examples.casual: No manches, ¿otra vez te subieron la renta?

notes: VULGAR Mexican slang. Same meaning as 'no manches' but crude; only with close friends who use it first. Never with family, bosses, strangers. Text: 'nmms'.

examples.tl: No mames, ¿ya son las tres de la mañana?
examples.en: No way, it's already three in the morning?

notes: Mexican all-purpose interjection: surprise ('¡Órale, qué grande!'), agreement ('Órale, ahí nos vemos'), or urging ('¡Órale, apúrate!'). Casual, not vulgar.

examples.tl: —Te invito a cenar el viernes. —¡Órale, va!
examples.en: —Dinner's on me Friday. —Oh nice, deal!

notes: Mexican. Means 'exactly / that's right', 'hurry up', or 'ok, deal' ('Ándale, pues'). Friendly. 'Ándale' is also what the cartoon Speedy Gonzales says.

examples.tl: —¿La farmacia de la esquina? —¡Ándale, esa!
examples.en: —The pharmacy on the corner? —Yes, that one exactly!

notes: Mexican mild interjection for 'oh no / jeez', often before bad news or an apology ('Híjole, no voy a poder'). Clean; grandmothers say it.

examples.tl: Híjole, se me olvidó pagar el internet.
examples.en: Oh man, I forgot to pay the internet bill.
examples.casual: Híjole, se me olvidó pagar el internet.

notes: Universal interjection for a small shock, mistake or sympathy ('Uy, qué mal'). Colombians use 'uy' constantly ('¡Uy, qué chévere!').

examples.tl: ¡Uy, perdón! No te vi.
examples.en: Oops, sorry! I didn't see you.

notes: Pain, annoyance, tenderness ('ay, qué bonito'), or frustration. 'Ay, Dios' and 'ay, no' are everyday. Spelled 'ay', not 'hay' (there is).

examples.tl: Ay, me pisaste.
examples.en: Ouch, you stepped on me.

notes: Dismay or refusal with feeling ('Ay no, yo no voy'). Very frequent in Mexican and Colombian texting, often stretched: 'ay nooo'.

examples.tl: Ay, no, otra vez se cayó el internet.
examples.en: Oh no, the internet went down again.
examples.casual: Ay nooo, otra vez se cayó el internet.

en: oh well / nothing to be done
notes: Mexican/Central American shrug of acceptance. 'Ni modo que…' = no way that… ('Ni modo que camine') is a different, sarcastic use.

examples.tl: Se canceló el vuelo. Ni modo, mañana salimos.
examples.en: The flight got cancelled. Oh well, we leave tomorrow.
examples.casual: Se canceló el vuelo, ni modo.

notes: Mexican for 'cool', all ages, totally clean. 'Está padre' = it's cool; 'padrísimo' = super cool. Outside Mexico it sounds odd (padre = father).

examples.tl: ¡Qué padre tu departamento, tiene mucha luz!
examples.en: Your apartment is so cool, it gets lots of light!

notes: Mexican slang, younger and more street than 'qué padre' but not vulgar. 'Está chido' = it's cool; 'chido' alone = cool / ok.

examples.tl: Está chido el bar, hay música en vivo.
examples.en: The bar is cool, there's live music.
examples.casual: Está chido el bar, hay música en vivo.

notes: The neutral reaction to good news anywhere in Latin America. 'Qué bueno que viniste' = good thing you came.

examples.tl: ¿Ya te dieron la visa? ¡Qué bueno!
examples.en: They gave you the visa already? That's great!
examples.casual: ¿Ya te dieron la visa? Q bueno!

notes: Neutral sympathy for bad news. Stronger: 'qué gacho' (Mex slang), 'qué horrible'.

examples.tl: ¿Te robaron el celular? Qué mal.
examples.en: They stole your phone? That sucks.

en: what a shame / what a pity
casual: Qué lástima que no puedas venir
notes: Neutral, slightly softer and more formal than 'qué mal'. Often 'qué lástima que + subjunctive'.

examples.tl: Qué lástima que cerraron esa taquería.
examples.en: What a shame they closed that taco place.
examples.casual: Q lástima q cerraron esa taquería.

notes: Neutral everywhere. Also 'qué extraño'. Mexican slang alternative: 'qué loco'.

examples.tl: Qué raro, el Uber dice que ya llegó pero no lo veo.
examples.en: Weird, the Uber says it arrived but I don't see it.
examples.casual: Q raro, el Uber dice q ya llegó.

notes: In Mexico/Colombia/Central America 'pena' = embarrassment, so 'qué pena' = how embarrassing or a polite 'sorry to bother'. In Spain/Argentina it means sadness.

examples.tl: Qué pena, se me olvidó tu nombre.
examples.en: How embarrassing, I forgot your name.
examples.casual: Q pena, se me olvidó tu nombre.

notes: From Arabic 'inshallah'. Alone = 'I hope so'; with a clause it takes the subjunctive: 'Ojalá que no llueva'. Universal.

examples.tl: —¿Crees que te den el trabajo? —Ojalá.
examples.en: —Think they'll give you the job? —Hopefully.

notes: Agreement or 'naturally'. 'Claro que sí' = of course; 'claro que no' = of course not. Neutral, all countries.

examples.tl: —¿Me ayudas con las bolsas? —Claro.
examples.en: —Can you help me with the bags? —Sure.

notes: Casual, a bit sassy, popular with younger speakers. 'Obviamente' is the neutral adverb. 'Obvio, ¿no?' = duh, right?

examples.tl: —¿Vas a ir al concierto? —Obvio.
examples.en: —Are you going to the concert? —Obviously.

notes: Mexican colloquial, from '¡no, hombre!'. Emphatic no, or 'don't mention it'. Spoken and texted ('nombre'); sounds like 'nombre' (name) but isn't.

examples.tl: —¿Te molesto si llego a las diez? —¡Nombre, para nada!
examples.en: —Is it a bother if I arrive at ten? —Nah, not at all!

notes: Mexican 'ok / sounds good', from 'salir'. Also 'sale y vale', 'sale pues'. Very frequent in texts. Not used in Colombia or Central America.

examples.tl: —Te paso a buscar a las ocho. —Sale.
examples.en: —I'll pick you up at eight. —Ok.

notes: Mexican short 'ok' for agreeing to a plan. '¿Va?' = deal? Also 'va que va'. Very common in WhatsApp.

examples.tl: —¿Nos vemos en el Oxxo a las seis? —Va.
examples.en: —Meet at the Oxxo at six? —Ok.
examples.casual: Va, a las 6 en el Oxxo.

notes: The 'ok / go for it' of Colombia, Argentina, Venezuela, Caribbean. Mexicans understand it but say 'sale'/'va'. Also 'dale pues'.

examples.tl: —Te mando la dirección por WhatsApp. —Dale.
examples.en: —I'll send you the address on WhatsApp. —Ok.

notes: 'Ready' or 'done'. In Colombia 'listo' also = ok / got it (very frequent). '¿Listo?' = ready? Everyone understands it.

examples.tl: Listo, ya te hice la transferencia.
examples.en: Done, I already sent you the transfer.

notes: Tiny but everywhere: 'ya' = already/now ('ya llegué'), 'ok, got it' ('ya, ya'), or 'stop it' ('¡ya!'). '¿Ya?' = done yet?

examples.tl: —¿Ya terminaste? —Ya.
examples.en: —Are you done yet? —Yes, done.

notes: Marks completion: a form finished, a fix made, a deal closed. In Mexico 'ya quedó' is even more common for 'it's done/fixed'.

examples.tl: Ya está, pagué la renta y mandé el comprobante.
examples.en: Done, I paid the rent and sent the receipt.
examples.casual: Ya está, ya pagué y mandé el comprobante.

notes: 'See? I told you' with a bit of 'I was right'. Also softer: 'ya ves cómo es' = you know how it is. 'Ya ve' for usted.

examples.tl: Ya ves, te dije que el metro era más rápido.
examples.en: See, I told you the metro was faster.
examples.casual: Ya ves, te dije q el metro era más rápido.

notes: Resigned or reflective agreement. 'Pues no' is the opposite. Mexican speech: 'pus sí'.

examples.tl: —Está caro, pero vale la pena. —Pues sí.
examples.en: —It's expensive but worth it. —Yeah, I guess.

notes: Reply to '¿qué haces?' or '¿qué pasó?'. 'Nada, nada' = never mind. 'De nada' = you're welcome. 'Pues nada' = anyway / so yeah.

examples.tl: —¿Qué tienes? —Nada, estoy cansado.
examples.en: —What's wrong? —Nothing, I'm tired.

notes: Mexican slang, from the letter X. 'Está equis' = it's meh; 'equis' alone = whatever, doesn't matter. Casual, clean. Text: 'x'.

examples.tl: —¿Qué tal la película? —Equis, nada especial.
examples.en: —How was the movie? —Meh, nothing special.

casual: Me vale, que haga lo que quiera
notes: Mexican. Short for a vulgar phrase ('me vale madre(s)'), but 'me vale' alone is mild, like 'I couldn't care less'. Don't say it to someone complaining to you.

examples.tl: Me vale si llueve, de todos modos voy.
examples.en: I don't care if it rains, I'm going anyway.

notes: VULGAR Mexican slang. Enthusiastic yes ('¡A huevo que voy!') or 'by force' ('a huevo tuve que pagar'). Friends only; crude in mixed company. Text: 'a webo'.

examples.tl: —¿Vas al partido el domingo? —¡A huevo!
examples.en: —Going to the game Sunday? —Hell yeah!

notes: Mexican slang 'yes', playful and street. Not vulgar but very informal; say it only with friends. Opposite: 'nel'.

examples.tl: —¿Traes dinero? —Simón, yo pago.
examples.en: —Got money on you? —Yep, I'll pay.

notes: Mexican slang 'no'. Casual, a little rough-and-tumble, common in texts among friends. 'Nel pastel' is a jokey longer version.

examples.tl: —¿Vienes a la fiesta? —Nel, tengo que trabajar.
examples.en: —Coming to the party? —Nope, I have to work.

notes: Mexican slang for disappointment or disbelief ('Chale, perdí el camión'). Casual, not vulgar, mostly Mexico City and the north.

examples.tl: Chale, ya se acabaron los tacos de pastor.
examples.en: Damn, they ran out of pastor tacos.

notes: Mexican slang (literally strawberry): a rich, stuck-up or very proper person, also their way of talking ('o sea, güey'). Teasing, not vulgar. Noun: 'un fresa'.

examples.tl: Ese bar está lleno de fresas de Polanco.
examples.en: That bar is full of preppy kids from Polanco.
examples.casual: Ese bar está lleno de fresas.

notes: Mexican slang, OFFENSIVE: classist and often racist put-down meaning tacky/uncultured. You will hear it; do not use it on people. Opposite of 'fresa'.

examples.tl: Dicen que es naco poner la música a todo volumen en el metro.
examples.en: They say blasting music on the metro is tacky.
examples.casual: Qué naco poner la música así en el metro.

notes: Mexican slang for poor quality or fake ('un celular chafa'). Casual, not vulgar. Elsewhere: 'de mala calidad', Colombia 'chimbo'.

examples.tl: No compres ese cargador, es muy chafa y se rompe luego.
examples.en: Don't buy that charger, it's junk and breaks fast.
examples.casual: No compres ese cargador, está bn chafa.

notes: Mexican, superlative of 'padre'. Clean, all ages ('la boda estuvo padrísima'). Agrees in gender: padrísimo/padrísima.

examples.tl: El concierto estuvo padrísimo, deberías haber ido.
examples.en: The concert was awesome, you should have gone.

notes: VULGAR Mexican slang (from 'chingar'). Very positive: 'está chingón' = it's badass; 'eres un chingón' = you're great. Friends only; not with elders or at work.

examples.tl: Tu carro nuevo está chingón.
examples.en: Your new car is badass.

notes: VULGAR. Between close male friends = 'dude'/'badass'; about someone else = bastard; 'está cabrón' = it's hard/intense. Insulting to strangers. Mexico/Caribbean.

examples.tl: Está cabrón el examen de manejo, estudia bien.
examples.en: The driving test is brutal, study hard.

notes: Mexican 'dude', from 'buey' (ox). Texted as 'wey' or 'we'. Mildly vulgar: everywhere among young friends, but not for elders, bosses or strangers. Also = idiot.

examples.tl: ¿Qué onda, güey? ¿Dónde andas?
examples.en: What's up, dude? Where are you?

notes: Short for 'hermano'. Friendly, clean, Mexico and Central America; Colombia says 'hermano' or 'parce'. Diminutive 'manito'/'manita' is extra warm.

examples.tl: Gracias por la ayuda, mano, te debo una.
examples.en: Thanks for the help, bro, I owe you one.

notes: Mexican slang for a brother or a friend as close as one ('mi carnal'). Warm, working-class flavor, not vulgar. Feminine 'carnala'.

examples.tl: Te presento a mi carnal, crecimos juntos.
examples.en: Meet my bro, we grew up together.

notes: From 'compadre'. Friendly address for a male friend or even a stranger (vendor, mechanic) in Mexico and Central America. Clean. 'Comadre' for women.

examples.tl: ¿Cuánto por el kilo, compa?
examples.en: How much per kilo, buddy?

notes: Literal: boss. Mexican slang 'mi jefe/mi jefa' = my dad/my mom, affectionate. Also what vendors call customers: '¿Qué le damos, jefe?'. Not vulgar.

examples.tl: Voy a comer a casa de mi jefa el domingo.
examples.en: I'm having lunch at my mom's on Sunday.
examples.casual: Voy con mi jefa el domingo.

notes: Mexican colloquial surprise, milder than 'no manches'. '¿A poco sí?' = oh really? '¿A poco no?' = isn't it, though? Casual, clean.

examples.tl: ¿A poco ya cerraron el banco? Apenas son las tres.
examples.en: They already closed the bank? It's barely three.

notes: Mexican way to walk back a joke or a false statement ('…no te creas, es broma'). Texted as 'ntc'. 'No se crea' for usted.

examples.tl: Me voy a comer todos tus tacos… no te creas.
examples.en: I'm going to eat all your tacos… just kidding.
examples.casual: Me como todos tus tacos… ntc jaja

notes: Mexican colloquial for 'outright / without a doubt': 'De plano no me gustó'. Neutral register, very frequent in speech.

examples.tl: De plano me cambio de banco, me cobran de todo.
examples.en: I'm flat out switching banks, they charge me for everything.
examples.casual: De plano me cambio de banco.

en: right now / in a bit (maybe never)
notes: Mexican/Central American diminutive of ahora. Means 'right now', 'in a while' or 'never', depending on tone. 'Ahorita vengo' = be right back. Famously vague.

examples.tl: Ahorita te mando la foto del contrato.
examples.en: I'll send you the photo of the lease in a sec.

casual: Qué oso, me caí frente a todos
notes: Mexican slang (literally 'what a bear') for an embarrassing moment: 'hice un oso' = I embarrassed myself. Colombia also uses 'qué oso'. Casual, clean.

examples.tl: Le dije 'mamá' a la maestra. ¡Qué oso!
examples.en: I called the teacher 'mom'. So embarrassing!
examples.casual: Le dije mamá a la maestra, q oso.

notes: Mexican colloquial 'almost there / almost done'. 'Ya merito' is even more casual. Elsewhere: 'ya casi'. Like ahorita, treat the timing with suspicion.

examples.tl: —¿Ya está la comida? —Ya mero.
examples.en: —Is the food ready? —Almost.

notes: The 'cool' of Colombia, Venezuela, Caribbean, Ecuador, Peru. Clean, all ages. Not used in Mexico (they say 'padre'/'chido') but understood.

examples.tl: ¡Qué chévere que vengas a Medellín en diciembre!
examples.en: How cool that you're coming to Medellín in December!
examples.casual: Q chévere q vengas en diciembre!

notes: Colombian slang from 'parcero' (partner). Casual, clean, used constantly among friends in Colombia. Mexico's equivalents: güey (vulgar-ish), compa, carnal.

examples.tl: Parce, ¿me prestas diez mil para el bus?
examples.en: Dude, can you lend me ten thousand for the bus?

notes: Strong surprise, good or bad ('¡Qué bárbaro, qué bien cantas!' / '¡Qué bárbaro, qué calor!'). Neutral, a touch old-fashioned; common with older speakers.

examples.tl: ¡Qué bárbaro! Tres horas de fila en migración.
examples.en: Unbelievable! Three hours in line at immigration.

notes: Texting shorthand for 'que/qué'. Universal in WhatsApp; most adults still write 'que'. Older variant 'k' (ke). Accents and ¿ are dropped in fast texting.

examples.tl: ¿q onda? ¿q vas a hacer hoy?
examples.en: what's up? what are you doing today?

notes: 'x' = por (from the multiplication sign), so 'xq' = porque/por qué. 'pq' is the other common form, more Colombia/Spain. Casual texting only.

examples.tl: ¿xq no contestas? Te marqué tres veces.
examples.en: why aren't you answering? I called you three times.
examples.casual: xq no contestas, te marqué 3 veces

notes: 'tb', 'tmb' and 'tbn' all = también. 'Yo tb' = me too. Universal texting shorthand; also 'tampoco' becomes 'tmpco' sometimes.

examples.tl: —Tengo hambre. —Yo tb, ¿vamos x tacos?
examples.en: —I'm hungry. —Me too, tacos?

notes: Texting shorthand for 'bien'. 'Todo bn' = all good; 'está bn' = it's fine. Universal but mostly younger texters.

examples.tl: —¿cómo estás? —bn y tú?
examples.en: —how are you? —good and you?

notes: Old-school texting 'que' from the SMS era ('k onda', 'xk'). Still seen but feels 2010 or looks like a typo for 'ok'. Young people now write 'q' or just 'que'.

examples.tl: ¿k onda? ¿todo bn?
examples.en: what's up? all good?

notes: Clipped 'por favor'. Spoken and texted everywhere, friendly; 'porfis' is cutesy, 'xfa' is pure texting. With officials or elders use the full 'por favor'.

examples.tl: Pásame la ubicación, porfa.
examples.en: Send me the location, please.

notes: 'Te quiero mucho', for friends, family, partners. 'tkm' is the same (older spelling). 'tq' = te quiero. 'Te amo' is stronger, romantic.

examples.tl: Gracias por todo, tqm.
examples.en: Thanks for everything, love you lots.

notes: Same as 'tqm' with the SMS-era 'k'. Still common, especially among people who texted in the 2000s. Both are fine.

examples.tl: Feliz cumple, tkm.
examples.en: Happy birthday, love you lots.

notes: 'No te preocupes'. Very common Mexican texting reply to an apology or a worry. Spoken version: 'no te preocupes' or 'no hay bronca' (Mex slang).

examples.tl: —Perdón, llego 10 min tarde. —ntp, aquí te espero.
examples.en: —Sorry, I'll be 10 min late. —No worries, I'll wait here.

en: no te apures (no rush, don't worry)
notes: 'No te apures' = don't hurry / don't worry, Mexican. Less common than 'ntp'; some people read 'nta' as 'neta', so context matters.

examples.tl: —Voy tarde. —nta, no hay prisa.
examples.en: —I'm running late. —No rush, no hurry.

notes: Spanish laughs with 'j' (jaja), never 'haha'. More 'ja' = funnier; 'jajajaja' is normal. 'jsjsjs' is Gen-Z, 'jeje' is sly, 'lol' is rare, 'xd' also used.

examples.tl: jajaja no puede ser, mándame la foto
examples.en: hahaha no way, send me the photo

notes: Universal. A bare 'ok' can read as cold in a chat, like in English; people soften it: 'ok va', 'okey', 'ok, gracias', 'oki'.

examples.tl: Ok, nos vemos a las 8 entonces.
examples.en: Ok, see you at 8 then.

notes: Playful, friendly 'ok' in texts, more common from women and young people. 'okis' is the same. Avoid in work chats.

examples.tl: —Te veo abajo en 5. —oki
examples.en: —See you downstairs in 5. —okie

notes: Texting shorthand for 'bueno'. Common in Mexico. Also 'bn' (bien) and 'bno' are easy to mix up; 'bno' usually opens or closes a topic.

examples.tl: bno, mañana te cuento todo
examples.en: ok, tomorrow I'll tell you everything

notes: 'Saludos' with the number 2 ('dos'). Playful SMS-era shorthand, now a bit dated or ironic but still seen in family WhatsApp groups.

examples.tl: Feliz año a todos, salu2 desde México
examples.en: Happy new year everyone, greetings from Mexico

notes: Texting shorthand for 'dónde'. 'dnd estás' / 'dnd andas' = where are you. Universal among young texters.

examples.tl: ¿dnd estás? ya llegué
examples.en: where are you? I'm here

notes: Texting shorthand for 'cuándo'. Less standardized than 'dnd' or 'xq'; you also see 'cuand', 'kndo'.

examples.tl: ¿qndo nos vemos? tengo libre el sábado
examples.en: when are we meeting? I'm free Saturday
examples.casual: qndo nos vemos, el sábado tengo libre

notes: 'x' = por (multiplication 'por'). 'x favor', 'x fin' (finally), 'x eso' (that's why), 'xq'. Also 'x' alone can mean 'equis' (whatever) in Mexico.

examples.tl: gracias x la ayuda, x fin quedó el wifi
examples.en: thanks for the help, the wifi finally works
examples.casual: gracias x todo, x fin quedó

notes: Texting shorthand for 'mañana'. The ñ is kept on Spanish keyboards; without it you may see 'mnn' or 'mnna'.

examples.tl: mñn te pago, hoy no me ha caído la quincena
examples.en: I'll pay you tomorrow, my paycheck hasn't come in today
examples.casual: mñn te pago, no me ha caído la quincena

notes: The old XD emoticon survives as a word in Latin American texting: lowercase 'xd' tagged on the end means 'lol / jk'. Very common with people under 30.

examples.tl: casi me quedo dormido en la junta xd
examples.en: I almost fell asleep in the meeting lol
examples.casual: casi me duermo en la junta xd

notes: Clipped 'estoy'; likewise 'tas' = estás, 'tamos' = estamos, 'ta' = está. Casual texting and fast speech across Latin America.

examples.tl: toy afuera, ¿bajas o subo?
examples.en: I'm outside, are you coming down or should I come up?

notes: SMS-era spelling of 'aquí'. Still seen but dated; most people now type 'aquí' or 'aqui'.

examples.tl: aki te espero afuera del Oxxo
examples.en: I'll wait for you here outside the Oxxo

notes: Shorthand for 'mensaje'. 'Mándame un msj' or 'wasap' = text me. Mexico also says 'mándame un whats'.

examples.tl: cuando llegues mándame un msj
examples.en: when you get there send me a message

notes: VULGAR Mexican texting shorthand for 'no mames'. Everywhere in young friends' chats, expressing shock or 'lmao'. Not for family or work groups.

examples.tl: nmms, me acaban de cancelar el vuelo
examples.en: no way, they just cancelled my flight

en: shall we meet up? / are we on?
notes: 'Quedar' = to arrange to meet. 'Quedamos a las 8' = we're on for 8; '¿en qué quedamos?' = so what did we decide? Mexico often prefers 'vernos'.

examples.tl: Entonces, ¿quedamos el viernes en tu casa?
examples.en: So, are we on for Friday at your place?

notes: The everyday way to propose meeting. '¿Nos vemos en la tarde?' Add 'para + verb': 'nos vemos para cenar'.

examples.tl: ¿Nos vemos más tarde para un café?
examples.en: Want to meet later for a coffee?
examples.casual: ¿Nos vemos más tarde x un café?

notes: One-word question when planning. Follow-ups: '¿Dónde exactamente?', 'Mándame la ubicación'. Texting: 'dnd'.

examples.tl: —Vamos a cenar. —Va, ¿dónde?
examples.en: —Let's have dinner. —Ok, where?

notes: Standard. Answer with 'a las + hour': 'a las siete y media'. 'A qué horas' (plural) is common colloquial Mexican.

examples.tl: ¿A qué hora llegas al aeropuerto?
examples.en: What time do you get to the airport?

notes: Casual way to ask what's happening or propose doing something. Also '¿Qué planes?' / '¿Hay plan?'. Universal informal.

examples.tl: ¿Qué plan para el fin de semana?
examples.en: What's the plan for the weekend?

notes: 'Salir' = to go out (socially, or to leave). 'Salir con alguien' can mean dating. '¿Salimos a caminar?' is innocent.

examples.tl: ¿Salimos el sábado? Hay un bar nuevo en la Roma.
examples.en: Want to go out Saturday? There's a new bar in Roma.
examples.casual: ¿Salimos el sábado? Hay un bar nuevo.

notes: 'Invitar' = to treat. Important: if you say 'te invito a comer' you are paying. 'Yo pago' is the plainer version.

examples.tl: Vamos por unos tacos, yo invito.
examples.en: Let's get some tacos, my treat.

notes: Mexico/Central America say 'cada quien' (elsewhere 'cada uno'). Splitting the bill by item; 'a la americana' is also heard, with a smile.

examples.tl: Mejor cada quien paga lo suyo, ¿va?
examples.en: Better everyone pays their own, ok?

notes: Split the bill in half. 'Ir a medias' = go halves. Neutral everywhere. Also 'mitad y mitad', or 'dividimos la cuenta'.

examples.tl: ¿Vamos a medias con el Uber?
examples.en: Split the Uber fifty-fifty?

notes: 'Espérame' = hold on a sec, or wait for me. 'Espéreme' for usted. Also 'espera' / 'aguanta' (Mex, 'hang on').

examples.tl: Espérame cinco minutos, ya casi llego.
examples.en: Wait for me five minutes, I'm almost there.

notes: Neutral-polite. Diminutives soften it: 'un momentito', 'un segundo', 'un segundito'. Mexico: 'ahorita' also does the job.

examples.tl: Un momento, le reviso si tenemos su talla.
examples.en: One moment, I'll check if we have your size.
examples.casual: Un momentito, ya te lo paso.

notes: The standard text when you arrive. Also to confirm you got home safe: 'ya llegué a casa'. Reply: 'Qué bueno, descansa'.

examples.tl: Ya llegué, estoy en la entrada del edificio.
examples.en: I'm here, I'm at the building entrance.
examples.casual: Ya llegué, toy en la entrada.

notes: Universal 'almost (there/done)'. 'Ya casi llego' is the classic text sent from 20 minutes away. Mexico also 'ya mero'.

examples.tl: —¿Dónde estás? —Ya casi, estoy a dos cuadras.
examples.en: —Where are you? —Almost, I'm two blocks away.

notes: 'Estoy en camino' and 'voy en camino' are interchangeable; 'ya voy' is the shortest. Often sent before you have actually left.

examples.tl: Estoy en camino, el tráfico está horrible.
examples.en: I'm on my way, traffic is horrible.
examples.casual: Voy en camino, hay un tráfico horrible.

notes: Slightly more common than 'estoy en camino' in Mexican texting. 'Ya voy' = coming / on it. 'Voy saliendo' = just leaving.

examples.tl: Voy en camino, llego en diez minutos.
examples.en: On my way, I'll be there in ten minutes.

notes: The universal (and rarely true) ETA. 'Dame cinco minutos' = give me five. 'Cinco minutitos' makes the lie cuter.

examples.tl: Dame cinco minutos, me estoy cambiando.
examples.en: Give me five minutes, I'm getting changed.

notes: 'Andar' = to be around, moving. More casual than '¿dónde estás?' and very Mexican/Central American. Also '¿Por dónde andas?'.

examples.tl: ¿Dónde andas? Te estamos esperando en la mesa.
examples.en: Where are you? We're waiting for you at the table.
examples.casual: ¿Dnd andas? Te esperamos en la mesa.

notes: Neutral everywhere. '¿Dónde está?' for usted. 'Estar' for location, never 'ser'.

examples.tl: ¿Dónde estás? El Uber ya llegó.
examples.en: Where are you? The Uber is here.

en: you're so slow! / that took forever
notes: Mexican: 'tardado' = slow, taking long (about a person or process). Playful complaint between friends. Elsewhere: 'qué demorado' (Colombia), 'qué lento'.

examples.tl: ¡Qué tardado! Llevo media hora esperándote.
examples.en: You're so slow! I've been waiting half an hour.
examples.casual: Q tardado, llevo media hora aquí.

notes: 'Tener hambre', never 'estar hambriento' in casual speech. Intensify: 'tengo mucha hambre', 'me muero de hambre', Mexican slang 'tengo un hambre canija'.

examples.tl: Tengo hambre, ¿vamos por algo?
examples.en: I'm hungry, want to grab something?

notes: In Mexico 'comer' also = to have the main midday meal (2–4 pm), so 'vamos a comer' often means lunch. 'Vamos a cenar' = dinner.

examples.tl: Vamos a comer, conozco una fonda buenísima aquí cerca.
examples.en: Let's go eat, I know a great little lunch place nearby.
examples.casual: Vamos a comer, hay una fonda buenísima cerca.

notes: Mexican slang 'chela' = beer. Also 'unas cheves', 'unas frías'. Colombia: 'unas polas'. Casual, friendly, clean.

examples.tl: Terminando la chamba vamos por unas chelas.
examples.en: After work let's go grab some beers.

notes: Mexican slang for cerveza, used by everyone, clean. 'Cheve' is the northern variant. Colombia: 'pola'; Central America: 'birra' (also used widely).

examples.tl: ¿Me das una chela bien fría, por favor?
examples.en: Can I get a nice cold beer, please?

notes: 'Trago' = a (hard) drink. 'Vamos por unos tragos' = let's get drinks. Colombia: 'tomar unos tragos / unas polas'. Neutral everywhere.

examples.tl: ¿Vamos por unos tragos después de la cena?
examples.en: Want to get a few drinks after dinner?

notes: 'Descanso' (m) = break/rest. 'Descansa' = rest up (what you tell someone going to bed). 'Un break' is also heard in Mexico.

examples.tl: Llevo seis horas trabajando, voy a tomar un descanso.
examples.en: I've been working six hours, I'm taking a break.
examples.casual: Voy a descansar un rato, llevo 6 horas.

notes: 'Tener sueño' = be sleepy (not 'estoy sueño'). 'Tengo flojera' = I feel lazy (Mex). 'Estoy cansado' = I'm tired.

examples.tl: Tengo mucho sueño, me desvelé viendo la serie.
examples.en: I'm really sleepy, I stayed up late watching the show.
examples.casual: Tengo un sueño, me desvelé con la serie.

notes: How you sign off a late chat. Short: 'ya me duermo'. Reply: 'Descansa' / 'Que descanses' / 'Dulces sueños'.

examples.tl: Ya me voy a dormir, mañana me levanto a las seis.
examples.en: I'm going to bed, I'm up at six tomorrow.
examples.casual: Ya me duermo, mñn me levanto a las 6.

notes: Neutral everywhere. 'Que tengas buen viaje' is the fuller form. 'Buen vuelo' for a flight. Often followed by 'avísame cuando llegues'.

examples.tl: ¡Buen viaje! Mándame foto cuando aterrices.
examples.en: Have a good trip! Send me a photo when you land.
examples.casual: Buen viaje! Mándame foto cuando aterrices.

notes: What you say to someone leaving, driving or walking home at night: 'vete con cuidado', 'maneja con cuidado'. Warm, neutral.

examples.tl: Ya es tarde, vete con cuidado y avísame.
examples.en: It's late, be careful on your way and let me know.
examples.casual: Ya es tarde, con cuidado y avísame.

en: sound good? / you up for it? (Mex)
notes: Mexican slang: 'latir' (to beat) used for 'to appeal to'. 'Me late' = I'm into it; 'no me late' = not feeling it. Casual, clean.

examples.tl: Pensaba ir a Coyoacán el domingo, ¿te late?
examples.en: I was thinking of going to Coyoacán Sunday, you up for it?

notes: Ask after someone's event or day. '¿Cómo le fue?' for usted. Answer: 'Me fue bien / mal / más o menos'.

examples.tl: ¿Cómo te fue en migración? ¿Te dieron la cita?
examples.en: How did it go at immigration? Did they give you the appointment?

notes: Mexican 'marcar' = to dial/call. 'Te llamo' is universal; Colombia 'te timbro'. 'Nos hablamos' = we'll be in touch.

examples.tl: Ahorita no puedo hablar, te marco en una hora.
examples.en: I can't talk right now, I'll call you in an hour.
examples.casual: No puedo hablar, te marco en 1 hora.

notes: WhatsApp location pin. 'La ubi' is the universal shortening. Also 'compárteme tu ubicación' when you want live location.

examples.tl: No encuentro el lugar, mándame la ubicación.
examples.en: I can't find the place, send me the location.
examples.casual: No lo encuentro, mándame la ubi.

notes: The everyday 'sorry' for bumping into someone, interrupting, or a small mistake. Also '¿Perdón?' = pardon? Neutral, all countries.

examples.tl: Perdón, ¿me dejas pasar?
examples.en: Sorry, can I get by?

notes: 'Disculpa' (tú) / 'disculpe' (usted). The polite way to get a stranger's attention or apologize lightly. 'Disculpe' is what you say to a waiter or official.

examples.tl: Disculpe, ¿dónde queda la oficina de migración?
examples.en: Excuse me, where is the immigration office?

notes: For real regret or sympathy (bad news, a death, a genuine mistake). For bumping into someone use 'perdón'. 'Lo siento mucho' = I'm so sorry.

examples.tl: Lo siento mucho, no sabía que estabas enfermo.
examples.en: I'm so sorry, I didn't know you were sick.
examples.casual: Lo siento, no sabía q estabas enfermo.

notes: Very Mexican: 'una disculpa' as a standalone apology, slightly formal-polite (customer service, texts to a landlord). 'Mil disculpas' = many apologies.

examples.tl: Una disculpa por la tardanza, había mucho tráfico.
examples.en: Apologies for the delay, there was a lot of traffic.
examples.casual: Una disculpa x la tardanza, mucho tráfico.

notes: Said when squeezing past people on the metro, a bus or a crowded market. Neutral everywhere. Fuller: 'con permiso'.

examples.tl: Permiso, bajo en la siguiente.
examples.en: Excuse me, I'm getting off at the next stop.
examples.casual: Permiso, bajo en la que sigue.

notes: Used when entering a room, leaving a table, or passing. Mexicans say it constantly; reply 'Propio' (Mex) or 'Pase / adelante'.

examples.tl: Con permiso, voy al baño.
examples.en: Excuse me, I'm going to the restroom.

notes: Formal (usted) request to pass, take something, or help ('¿Me permite su identificación?'). 'Me permites' with tú. Waiters use it when clearing plates.

examples.tl: ¿Me permite su pasaporte, por favor?
examples.en: May I have your passport, please?

notes: Say it more than you think you need to; Latin Americans thank cashiers, drivers, security guards. Texts: 'gracias!!', 'grax' (dated), 'grs'.

examples.tl: Gracias, que tenga buen día.
examples.en: Thanks, have a good day.

notes: Neutral everywhere. 'Muchísimas gracias' is stronger. Pair with the person: 'muchas gracias, señora', 'gracias, joven'.

examples.tl: Muchas gracias por recogerme en el aeropuerto.
examples.en: Thank you very much for picking me up at the airport.

notes: Warm, slightly informal 'thanks so much', very common in texts across Latin America. 'Un millón de gracias' is the bigger version.

examples.tl: Mil gracias por la recomendación del dentista.
examples.en: Thanks a million for the dentist recommendation.
examples.casual: Mil gracias x la reco del dentista.

notes: Closing a text or conversation after a favor. 'Gracias otra vez' is the same. Neutral.

examples.tl: Ya llegué bien a casa, gracias de nuevo por el aventón.
examples.en: I got home fine, thanks again for the ride.
examples.casual: Ya llegué, gracias de nuevo x el aventón.

notes: The default everywhere. Alternatives: 'no hay de qué', 'por nada' (Mex), 'con gusto' (Colombia/Central America), 'a la orden' (Colombia).

examples.tl: —Gracias por la ayuda. —De nada, para eso estamos.
examples.en: —Thanks for the help. —You're welcome, that's what we're here for.

notes: Slightly warmer and more old-fashioned than 'de nada'. Neutral across countries. Don't confuse with 'no hay de que' (no accent) in writing: accent on qué.

examples.tl: —Mil gracias por traerme. —No hay de qué.
examples.en: —Thanks a million for bringing me. —Don't mention it.
examples.casual: No hay de qué, cuando quieras.

notes: Mexican casual 'you're welcome' (literally 'for nothing'). Very common in shops and taxis. Elsewhere it may sound odd; 'de nada' is safe everywhere.

examples.tl: —Gracias, joven. —Por nada, que le vaya bien.
examples.en: —Thanks, young man. —No problem, take care.
examples.casual: Por nada, q te vaya bn.

notes: 'You're welcome' or 'happy to' in Colombia, Costa Rica, Guatemala and the rest of Central America. Mexicans use it too, mostly in service settings.

examples.tl: —Gracias por la información. —Con gusto, señor.
examples.en: —Thanks for the information. —Gladly, sir.
examples.casual: Con gusto, cualquier cosa me dices.

notes: Colombia (also Venezuela, Ecuador, Caribbean): shopkeepers call it out to offer help, and it also means 'you're welcome'. Mexico says 'a sus órdenes' instead.

examples.tl: —Gracias por el cambio. —A la orden, vecino.
examples.en: —Thanks for the change. —You're welcome, neighbor.

notes: Mexican: inviting someone into your home or shop ('pásale, siéntate'). 'Pase' / 'pásele' for usted. Elsewhere: 'adelante', 'entra', 'sigue' (Colombia).

examples.tl: ¡Hola! Pásale, estás en tu casa.
examples.en: Hi! Come in, make yourself at home.

notes: 'Siéntate' (tú) / 'siéntese' (usted). Hosts say it right after 'pásale'. 'Toma asiento' is more formal. Colombia: 'siga y se sienta'.

examples.tl: Siéntate, ahorita te traigo un café.
examples.en: Have a seat, I'll bring you a coffee in a sec.

notes: Mexican politeness: offering food or drink with one word. 'Gusta' for usted. Also said by people eating when you walk by; polite reply 'Gracias, provecho'.

examples.tl: Estamos comiendo pozole, ¿gustas?
examples.en: We're having pozole, would you like some?

notes: The basic host offer. '¿Quiere agua?' for usted. In Mexico 'agua' may mean agua fresca (flavored water); ask for 'agua natural' or 'agua sola' for plain.

examples.tl: Siéntate, ¿quieres agua o un refresco?
examples.en: Have a seat, do you want water or a soda?

notes: Said to anyone eating, even strangers at the next table, as you arrive or leave. Mexico: 'provecho'; elsewhere 'buen provecho'. Reply 'gracias' or 'igualmente'.

examples.tl: —Provecho. —Gracias, igualmente.
examples.en: —Enjoy your meal. —Thanks, you too.

notes: The all-purpose reply to good wishes: 'que te vaya bien' → 'igualmente'; 'provecho' → 'igualmente'; 'mucho gusto' → 'igualmente'. Short: 'igual'.

examples.tl: —Mucho gusto. —Igualmente.
examples.en: —Nice to meet you. —Likewise.

notes: Present tense: you don't understand in general or right now. Soften with 'perdón, no entiendo' or 'no te entiendo bien'.

examples.tl: Perdón, no entiendo. ¿Me lo puede explicar otra vez?
examples.en: Sorry, I don't understand. Can you explain it again?

notes: Preterite: you missed that one sentence. More natural than 'no entiendo' when you just didn't catch something. 'No te entendí' = I didn't get you.

examples.tl: No entendí lo último, ¿cuánto dijo que cuesta?
examples.en: I didn't catch the last part, how much did you say it costs?

notes: The polite 'what?' when you didn't hear. Universal. '¿Qué?' alone is blunt and sounds rude to older people; Mexicans prefer '¿mande?'.

examples.tl: ¿Cómo? Hay mucho ruido, no te oigo.
examples.en: What? It's really noisy, I can't hear you.

notes: Mexican only, from 'mandar' (command me). The polite 'what did you say?' or response when called ('¡Lloyd!' '¿Mande?'). Elsewhere sounds servile; use '¿cómo?'.

examples.tl: —Oiga, señor. —¿Mande?
examples.en: —Excuse me, sir. —Yes?

notes: Rising intonation turns 'perdón' into 'pardon me, what?'. Neutral everywhere; can also signal offense ('¿Perdón?!') like English.

examples.tl: ¿Perdón? No le escuché bien.
examples.en: Pardon? I didn't hear you well.

notes: '¿Otra vez, por favor?' = again please. '¿Otra vez?' alone = again?! (annoyed). 'De nuevo' is the synonym.

examples.tl: ¿Me lo dice otra vez, por favor? Más despacio.
examples.en: Can you say that again, please? Slower.

notes: 'Repite' (tú) / 'repita' (usted). '¿Me lo repites?' is softer and more natural in conversation. Add 'por favor' always.

examples.tl: ¿Puede repetir la dirección, por favor?
examples.en: Can you repeat the address, please?

notes: Ask about a word you heard. '¿Qué quiere decir…?' is the same. Very useful with slang: '¿Qué significa güey?'.

examples.tl: ¿Qué significa 'ahorita'? ¿Ahora o después?
examples.en: What does 'ahorita' mean? Now or later?

notes: Ask for the Spanish word. '¿Cómo se dice X en español?' Everyone understands and likes to help.

examples.tl: ¿Cómo se dice 'landlord' en español?
examples.en: How do you say 'landlord' in Spanish?

notes: '¿Habla inglés?' for usted (strangers, officials). Open with 'Disculpe' to be polite. Many will answer 'un poco'.

examples.tl: Disculpe, ¿habla inglés? Es que mi español es básico.
examples.en: Excuse me, do you speak English? My Spanish is basic.

notes: 'Poquito' sounds humble and friendly; 'un poco de español' is the textbook form. Saying this earns patience and slower speech.

examples.tl: Hablo poquito español, ¿puede hablar más despacio?
examples.en: I speak a little Spanish, can you speak more slowly?
examples.casual: Hablo poquito español, más despacio porfa.

notes: Great opener; people will compliment you and often slow down. Add 'corrígeme si me equivoco' = correct me if I'm wrong.

examples.tl: Estoy aprendiendo español, corríjame si digo algo mal.
examples.en: I'm learning Spanish, correct me if I say something wrong.

notes: 'Despacio' = slowly. 'Más lento' also works. '¿Puede hablar más despacio?' is the full polite form.

examples.tl: ¿Puede hablar más despacio, por favor? Estoy aprendiendo.
examples.en: Can you speak more slowly, please? I'm learning.

notes: Checking you are doing something right: filling a form, pronouncing a word, folding a tortilla. Answer: 'Sí, así' or 'No, así no'.

examples.tl: ¿Así se escribe mi apellido? ¿Con dos eles?
examples.en: Is this how my last name is written? With two l's?

en: is that ok? / is it right?
notes: Both 'is this correct?' and 'is that ok with you?'. As a statement 'está bien' = fine / ok / it's good. '¿Todo bien?' checks on a person.

examples.tl: Llego a las nueve en vez de las ocho, ¿está bien?
examples.en: I'll arrive at nine instead of eight, is that ok?
examples.casual: Llego a las 9 en vez de las 8, ¿está bn?

notes: 'Está mal' = it's wrong / it's bad. 'Lo dije mal' = I said it wrong. 'Me siento mal' = I feel sick. 'Mal' is the adverb; 'malo' the adjective.

examples.tl: Creo que lo escribí mal, ¿me ayudas a corregirlo?
examples.en: I think I wrote it wrong, can you help me fix it?
examples.casual: Creo q lo escribí mal, ¿me ayudas?

notes: The 'oh, got it!' moment. 'Ya' marks the change from not understanding to understanding. Also 'ya, ya' or 'ah, ok'.

examples.tl: Ah, ya entendí, el camión pasa cada veinte minutos.
examples.en: Oh, got it, the bus comes every twenty minutes.

notes: Calm acknowledgment, also used to show empathy ('Entiendo, debe ser difícil'). 'Entendido' = understood (confirming an instruction).

examples.tl: Entiendo, entonces necesito la cita antes de pagar.
examples.en: I see, so I need the appointment before paying.
examples.casual: Entiendo, primero la cita y luego pago.

notes: Spelled 'no sé' with an accent (sé = I know; se = reflexive). In texts people often write 'nose' as one word. 'Quién sabe' = who knows.

examples.tl: No sé a qué hora abren, pregúntale al portero.
examples.en: I don't know what time they open, ask the doorman.
examples.casual: No sé a q hora abren, pregúntale al portero.

notes: Casual 'no clue', universal. 'No tengo ni idea' is the full form. 'Ni la menor idea' = not the faintest idea.

examples.tl: —¿Cuánto cuesta la visa? —Ni idea, búscalo en la página.
examples.en: —How much is the visa? —No idea, look it up on the site.
examples.casual: Ni idea, búscalo en la página.

notes: Acknowledging an explanation. Neutral, slightly reflective. 'Ah, ya' is the shorter Mexican version.

examples.tl: Ya veo, por eso el agua sale café los lunes.
examples.en: I see, that's why the water comes out brown on Mondays.
examples.casual: Ah ya veo, x eso sale café el agua.

notes: Literally 'do I explain myself?'. Used after explaining something to check it landed. Neutral; Mexicans also say '¿sí me entiendes?'.

examples.tl: Pago la mitad hoy y la otra en la quincena, ¿me explico?
examples.en: I pay half today and the rest on payday, does that make sense?
examples.casual: Mitad hoy y mitad en la quincena, ¿me explico?

notes: Casual Mexican tag, often just a filler like English 'you know?'. Also '¿me entiendes?' and, among friends, '¿captas?'.

examples.tl: No es que no quiera ir, es que no tengo lana, ¿sí me entiendes?
examples.en: It's not that I don't want to go, I just have no cash, you know?

notes: Essential at banks, pharmacies and immigration. Spelling aloud: 'con hache', 'doble ele', 'i griega' (y), 'be grande / be chica' (b/v, Mexico).

examples.tl: ¿Cómo se escribe su apellido? ¿Con be grande?
examples.en: How do you spell your last name? With a 'b'?
